THE LITE EDITION

*Three Ideas. Ten Steps. One Song.*

Before you dive into the full engine, here are the three ideas it runs
on and a ten-step path to a finished song. If you only use these three
ideas and nothing else, your songs will already be better.

Idea 1: The 1/f Boundary

The brain is a prediction engine. It builds a model of what comes next
and releases dopamine when that model is violated in a satisfying way. A
song that never surprises is boring. A song that never delivers on its
promises is noise. The boundary between them --- where pattern and
surprise coexist --- is where songs become unforgettable.

The engine measures every dimension of your song against this boundary
and tells you where you've drifted toward kitsch or chaos.

Idea 2: The Departure Budget

Every song has a budget of departures from its established pattern.
Spend the budget wisely --- one big surprise at the right moment, not
five medium surprises that cancel each other out. The chorus is a
departure from the verse. The bridge is a departure from both. Every
modulation, dynamic shift, and unexpected chord costs something. The
engine tracks what you've spent and what you have left.

Idea 3: Carrier and Payload

Charles Wesley wrote some of the most theologically dense lyrics in
English and set them to tunes congregations already knew. The tune was
the carrier. The content was the payload. The carrier's job was to
disappear.

A maximally simple harmonic carrier (the I--V--vi--IV loop you've heard
a thousand times) can hold a maximally heavy payload --- if the lyric is
doing real work. The engine keeps you from pairing simple harmony with
simple content.

The Ten-Step Workflow

Upload the full engine to your AI of choice and use this as your session
map:

> 1. Give your seed. One line. An emotion, an image, a title, or a
> lyric tension.
>
> 2. Name the tension. What are the two true things in this song
> that refuse to resolve? The tension is the engine's fuel.
>
> 3. Choose the song type. Lament? Anthem? Love song? Blues?
> Worship? The engine's Module 0 routes you to the right template.
>
> 4. Set the harmonic carrier. Simple and synchronizing. The room
> needs to lock in before you can depart from it.
>
> 5. Build the departure map. Where will the song leave the pattern?
> Verse→Chorus departure, Bridge departure. Spend the budget
> intentionally.
>
> 6. Write the melody arc. Interval pyramid: mostly small steps, one
> large leap at the emotional peak. Local reversal, global coherence.
>
> 7. Lyric skeleton. Title in the hook position. Tension named
> without resolution. Mouth test every line.
>
> 8. Production notes. Instrumentation, dynamic arc, the designed
> silence before re-entry.
>
> 9. Run the diagnostic. The engine scores your song against the 1/f
> boundary across six dimensions. See where you drifted. Decide what to
> fix.
>
> 10. Finish the song. The engine does not write your song. It
> measures it. You write it.

*The full engine follows. Every module is available. Use what you need.*

# PART I: CORE PRINCIPLES

The axioms. They do not change between versions, only deepen.

1. Pattern comes first.

A song must establish a trustworthy pattern before it can meaningfully
depart from it. The pattern is the synchronization surface that allows a
room full of strangers to breathe, move, and sing together. Without it,
departure is chaos.

2. Meaning lives in departures.

A song that never departs from its pattern is comfortable and
forgettable. A song that departs at the right moment, in the right
dimension, with the right payload, changes the room.

3. Tension increases replay value.

A song built on a genuine lyric tension --- an irreducible emotional
contradiction --- rewards repeated listening because the tension is
never fully resolved. Each repetition surfaces a different facet.

4. The mouth test is non-negotiable.

If a line does not feel natural in a human mouth moving at singing
speed, it does not belong in the song. No exceptions for lyric
sophistication.

5. Tension powers the engine.

The lyric tension is not a songwriting trick. It is the truthful
structure of how humans experience meaning --- held between
contradictions that refuse easy resolution. The engine works because the
tension is real.

6. The room is the instrument.

A song performed live is performed by a room, not for a room. Every
design decision must account for the audience as a participating system.

7. The engine must not become a formula.

If every song the engine produces follows the same structure, the engine
has replaced one formula with another. The tension determines the form.
The engine provides defaults. The tension gets veto power.

8. Beauty is the channel.

Musical excellence is stewardship of the channel through which a song
reaches its audience. The 1/f boundary is the frequency at which a
critically organized stimulus meets a critically organized nervous
system. A song at the boundary opens that channel.

9. Complexity must be discoverable, not just present.

The familiarity-complexity interaction (Chmiel and Schubert, 2017) shows
that repeated listening moves the Wundt curve apex rightward toward
greater complexity. Design for discovery, not just impact. The depth
that reveals itself on the fifth listen is the mechanism of longevity.

10. The score is a tool, not a verdict.

The computational modules produce scores, not judgments. A spectral
exponent of β = 1.4 is information, not a grade. The songwriter decides
what to do with it. The engine measures. The artist interprets.

# PART III: THE CARRIER/PAYLOAD PRINCIPLE

Charles Wesley wrote lyrics of extraordinary sophistication and set them
to tunes the congregation already knew. The tune was the carrier. The
content was the payload. The carrier's job was to disappear.

Contemporary pop has learned the first half: the I--V--vi--IV loop is
the most learnable harmonic carrier in Western music. But it has not
learned the second half: if the carrier is maximally simple, the payload
must be maximally dense. Instead, the current chart pairs simple harmony
with simple content.

> *The engine's goal: emotionally loaded content on maximally
> synchronizing patterns, with departures timed to deliver the payload
> when the room is most open to receiving it.*

## 0.4 Type Bands and Invariants (v30)

The type chosen here now decides which bands the floor reads the melody
against. Window 51 found two kinds of band. Invariants hold in every
corpus and culture measured --- tessitura 0.44--0.58 of the range, steps
0.394--0.578 of intervals, leaps 0.087--0.195, a leap filled by reversal
0.43--0.73 of the time, the arch the commonest contour, nearly every
note in the scale --- and a melody outside them is outside melody, not
outside a genre. Gated measures differ by genre: range (pop 16.0--21.0
semitones, dance 17.0--21.0, ballad 12.0--14.0, hymn 10.0--14.0),
density, bar repetition (pop 0.22--0.558, hymn 0.0--0.3) and melody

songs); Type W, and Type A when the record is congregational, against

# MODULE 0 EXTENSION: SONG TYPE TRIAGE PROTOCOL

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  NEW IN V26 --- The entry point for all sessions. Run before any other
  module. Q0 (Sovereignty Question) + Q1--Q9 routing questions.

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------

The engine has nine fully developed song types, each with its own intake
protocol, departure budget defaults, structural template, and production
specification. A songwriter who already knows their type skips straight
to the relevant module. Most do not know their type. They have an image,
a feeling, a situation, a line --- and the type is downstream of that,
not upstream.

This triage protocol routes any songwriter to the correct type through a
short conversational sequence. It begins with one question that no other
part of the engine asks: what do you think this song is about? That
answer brackets everything that follows. Every downstream decision can
be checked against it.

> *The engine's job is to bring the artist's vision to life --- not to
> impose its own architecture on material that is already alive. The
> triage protocol holds the artist's answer to Q0 as the sovereign
> reference point throughout the session.*

The protocol has ten questions. Most sessions resolve at Q4 or Q5. The
full ten are available when the signals are genuinely ambiguous or when
the songwriter's answers conflict with each other.

## How to Run This Protocol

Ask one question at a time. Do not present the full list. Do not explain
the routing logic while running the triage --- the songwriter does not
need to know how the questions work, only that they lead somewhere
useful.

After each answer, assess: is the type clear? If yes, route and begin
type-specific intake. If not, ask the next question. The questions are
ordered from most discriminating to least --- earlier questions resolve
the majority of cases.

When a type is identified, confirm it: "Based on what you've told me,
this sounds like a [type] --- does that feel right?" If the
songwriter says no, return to the Q0 anchor and trace where the routing
diverged from their sense of the song.

Hybrid types are common and valid. When two types pull with roughly
equal force, name both: "This has the structure of a Lament but the
social weight of an Anthem --- that's a Type L/A hybrid. The primary
type determines which intake we run first." Always primary type first.

## Q0 --- The Sovereignty Question

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  Ask this before anything else. Before routing. Before type. Before
  structure.

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
| What do you think this song is about?                             |
|                                                                       |
| *No constraints. One sentence or ten. Whatever comes first.*          |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+

This is not the same question as "what type is this song?" It is prior
to that question. It captures the artist's own understanding --- or
suspicion, or instinct --- about what they are making. It may be fully
formed ("it's about the year after my mother died") or barely formed
("something about leaving but not being able to go"). Both are useful.
Both are recorded.

The Q0 answer serves three functions throughout the session:

1\. Reference point. When the engine's routing conflicts with the
artist's instinct, Q0 is the tiebreaker. If someone says "it's about
a specific person" but the triage points toward Anthem, ask: does an
Anthem serve this material, or does it erase the specificity that makes
it true?

2\. Constraint. The engine will generate options throughout the session.
Q0 is the filter applied to all of them: does this serve what the artist
said this song is about?

3\. Completion check. At the end of the session, return to Q0: does the
finished song deliver what the artist said it was about in the first
place? If not, something was lost in the process and the session is not
done.

> *Record the Q0 answer verbatim. Do not paraphrase it. The artist's
> exact words are the anchor --- not the engine's interpretation of
> them.*

## When the Answers Conflict

Conflict Type 1: Artist vs. Engine

The Q0 answer points one direction and the routing questions point
another. Resolution: trust Q0. Ask directly: "Does the engine's
routing serve your vision, or does it replace it?" Let the artist
decide. Do not override Q0 with structural preference.

Conflict Type 2: Structure vs. Feeling

The structural signals suggest one type but Q7 (body) suggests another.
Resolution: the body question is often more honest than the cognitive
questions. Ask: "Where does this land in you when you sing it?" The
answer usually resolves the conflict.

Conflict Type 3: Genuine Hybrid

The answers are consistent but point to two types with equal force.
Resolution: name both and ask which is primary. "If you had to choose
--- that the body moves or that the two truths are held --- which would
you choose?" The primary type determines which intake runs first.

## 10.2 Verse Construction Rules

Rule V1: Physical Imagery in Every Line

Rule V1 amended again (v58, Window 76, fix 5): the writer's phrase;
the picture rule as a death the room may switch on. The writer chose
'no names --- the ones who knew me' for song 13's third verse; three
lines built on his wording died to Rule V1 (no concrete word), one of
them written twice, among five Rule V1 deaths in that slot (the run's
own report said five; its pool says three); the one survivor put the
phrase in a hand to pass the rule. v47 exempted the locked title's
words and the intake's objects from every word filter; a phrase the
writer picked at intake is the same kind of input. A WRITER'S PHRASE
(writer_phrases on the lines and lyric-first calls) is locked like the
title: a line carrying it is exempt from Rule V1 and from the word
filters and prints 'writer's wording' on its certificate. And Rule V1
itself is stated as the POLICY it is. Until v58 the app's scorer never
applied the picture rule as a death --- in the code 'Rule V1' deaths
were the weak-ending rule; the concrete-word requirement lived in the
paper and in the prompt, and the field reports applied it by hand (26
lines in song 11's writing room, 25 in song 8's, 14 in song 13's).
The writer's choice (the song 13 check): Rule V1 --- a concrete word
(Brysbaert ≥ 4.0, a plural or inflection read as its lemma), an object
of the intake or a name in every VERSE line --- is a death, ON by
default for verse slots; a pre-chorus line reports 'picture' and is
not killed (the run's reading, and the voice's declaratives); the
writer's phrase and a turn line are exempt; the writing room may switch
it off (picture_rule) as a stated choice, and every line reports
'picture' either way. 'I let the ones who knew me go' lives as
writer's wording; 'I let a few old friends go' dies to Rule V1.

Rule V1 amended a third time (v59, Window 77, fixes 4 and 8): the
couplet; the aside. With Rule V1 on, song 14's lines that set up the
last verse's turn died --- 'Paradise is out of sight' and three
versions of 'some will die', the setups of 'Not Harold though, for
the Savior he did cherish' --- and the run rewrote them with pictures.
v43 read the concrete ACT on the couplet; v58 read the picture on the
line alone. Rule V1 is now read on the COUPLET: a picture in the line
before or the line after satisfies it, and the line right before a turn
line is exempt; the certificate says when the couplet, not the line,
carries the image. And song 15's asides --- 'Nobody told me', 'I
spent a century down there', 'I know how that sounds', 'a little
embarrassed, a little grateful' --- are abstract on purpose: the
speaker turning to the listener. An ASIDE role (Table K's role table)

certificate prints the role, and the floor counts them per section. All

voice; the same line given the verse role still dies.

Every verse line must contain at least one concrete physical image ---
something the listener can touch, smell, see, or hear. No abstractions.
No conclusions. No statements of emotional state. Re-amended (v43, fix
1.1): PREFER a thing doing something --- a concrete noun with an action
verb (≥ 3.0) in the line or the line before --- but a still image is
allowed. The act is a bonus in Module 28's binding term, never a death:
applied as a death it killed a fifth of one song's candidates and most
of its understatement and list lines. The noun alone is null on the
chart; the noun doing something is hit-like (AUC 0.66, Window 59).

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  *Wrong: "He felt trapped and alone" --- this is a conclusion. Right:
  "He pours the same pot every morning, six forty-two" --- this is an
  experience. The listener draws the conclusion themselves.*

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------

Rule V2: IC-Entropy --- High Entropy in the Verse

Verse rhythm must be high-entropy: messy, conversational, slightly
off-beat, like speech falling toward something. Syllable counts between
paired verse lines should be close but not identical (target 6--9
syllables, inconsistent between pairs). Measured (Window 27): real verse
lines run 8.2 syllables at the median (hits 8.7), choruses 7.0; the
verse's type-token ratio is 0.58 against the chorus's 0.23, so the
entropy contrast is real and large. The 6--9 band holds; hits sit at its
top.

Rule V3: Contractions Close Phrases

Verse language uses contractions wherever natural speech would: he'd,
she'd, couldn't, wouldn't, ain't. Uncontracted forms add syllables
and lift the language into a register that feels written rather than
spoken. Measured (Window 27): contractions run at 5% of words in verses
and 5% in choruses alike, and no higher in hits. This is a register
instruction, not a verse/chorus rule, and it carries no evidence; keep
it as taste.

Rule V4: The Verse Is Pole A Territory

All verse imagery is drawn from the world described in Q2. The verse
does not reach toward Pole B. A verse that introduces resolution imagery
weakens the chorus arrival.

## 10.3 Chorus Construction Rules

Rule C1: Low Entropy --- Mirror the Syllables

Chorus lines must be low-entropy: clean rhythm, locked to the beat,
paired lines mirroring syllable counts at singing speed. Measured
(Window 27): confirmed in the strongest terms the corpus offers --- the
chorus's type-token ratio is below the verse's in 86% of songs; on the
page one chorus block repeats 28% of its own words, runs about six lines
of seven syllables, and uses commoner words than the verse (hits more
so). Rhyme (v12): 46% of line endings rhyme fully with another ending
within four lines, in every class of song, and the share does not
separate hits (Window 27) --- so rhyme is a floor, not a lever. The app
reads the scheme (AABB, ABAB, XAXA ...) and the full and loose densities
of each block; a block with no full rhyme and no loose rhyme is under
the floor.

Rule C2: The Convergence Word

The last word of every chorus is the convergence word. It must: (1) end
on an open vowel or liquid consonant; (2) be one syllable if possible;
(3) land on the structural tone (scale degree 5) and be held 3--5
seconds; (4) be marked [HOLD] in all documentation.

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  *Prohibited convergence words: any word ending in a closed consonant
  --- back, out, grip, lost, stuck, left, found, missed, past. These do
  not sustain on the open vowel the convergence tone requires.*

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------

Rule C3: The POV Contract

The song establishes a point-of-view contract in the first verse and
must honor it throughout. An unannounced POV shift mid-chorus that
changes whose interior the listener is in is a structural failure.

Rule C4: Same Melody, Three Times, Then Inversion

The chorus melody is fixed from the first occurrence. The final chorus
is the inversion: same melody, singer now knows what the first singer
did not.

## 10.4 The Inversion --- Final Chorus Construction

Same melody, same convergence word, different singer or knowledge state.
The world has been rotated 180 degrees and the same words now mean
something they could not have meant at the beginning. Specify the
inversion in Q7 before writing the first verse.

## 10.5 Bridge Construction Rules

The bridge is the rupture. It must be the single most exposed moment in
the song: fewest instruments, most tension, most specific language.
Bridge language is plainer and heavier than verse language. No wordplay.
Four lines maximum. Each line should feel like it cost something to
write.

## 10.9 The Ladder and the Object (v40, Window 58)

The engine writes the lines (Rule 11.16). These are the rules it writes
by for the line's meaning, each with its evidence; none is a weight
except the ladder's bonus in Module 28.

The ladder line. Climb the ladder in about one line in ten --- one
in two for a hymn. Put the feeling's object and the feeling in the same
line: a thing-word (door, scarf, rain, bread; Brysbaert ≥ 4.0) and a
meaning-word (love, truth, free, need, mercy; ≤ 2.5, a noun, verb or
adjective). Hits 0.1 of lines, uncharted 0.031, hymns 0.455. A lyric
that is all objects is a story; all meaning is a greeting card; the hits
do both at once and the hymns that last do it most. (Hayakawa 1939;
Eliot 1919; Pound 1913; Lakoff and Johnson 1980.)

The object. Choose the object before the line, then return to it.
The masters sit inside the chart's bands on every rate the app
measures; what the ear hears in them is which object and whether the
song came back --- hits name objects at the chart's rate and repeat
them (object TTR AUC 0.4). Two honest families: the storyteller names
many once (≥ 6.0 distinct concrete words per hundred --- Springsteen,
Dylan, Berry, Bowie); the feeler returns to a few (≤ 3.2 ---
Lennon--McCartney, Queen, Madonna). Pick one on purpose; the app names
which you wrote. (Kao and Jurafsky 2012; Pattison's object writing as
the practice that stocks the vocabulary.)

The register by type. Pop hits lean abstract (abstract share 0.403,
AUC 0.579); the hymns that last lean concrete (AUC 0.619). Name the
feeling outright somewhere in a pop lyric; name the thing the doctrine
lives in throughout a hymn. The imagery dial carries the tilt by type.

Temperature. Hits change temperature line to line more than
uncharted songs (valence SD 0.298 vs 0.222, AUC 0.704) --- warmer verses
and more cold lines. One line that goes cold against a warm chorus is
worth more than another warm one; the app names the coldest and warmest
lines. [Window 64: 0.529 on English only.]

When, and asking. A time word --- now, tonight, again, never,
always, forever, still --- about every nine lines (hits 0.112 per line,
uncharted none; AUC 0.695); it tells the listener where in their life
they are standing. About one line in thirty a question (AUC 0.643); a
question hands the chorus to the listener. [Window 64: 0.566 on English
only.] [Window 64: 0.511 on English only.]

# MODULE 23: HOOK ARCHITECTURE (CROSS-ENGINE INFRASTRUCTURE)

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  NEW IN V30 --- Applies to all eleven song types. Not a song type
  specification. A set of engineering constraints that operate beneath
  every module in the engine.

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------

## 23.1 Overview

Module 23 is not a song type template. It is infrastructure. Every
module in the engine assumes a hook is present. Module 23 is the first
to specify what a hook is, how to construct one, how to audit it, and
how to diagnose when it is failing. The constraints in this module apply
to every song produced by the engine regardless of type, subtype, or
production specification.

The module has three primary outputs: the Hook Specification (a
one-sentence description of the hook for any given song, naming its
location, its melodic feature, its lyric content, and its compound
elements), the Hook Audit (eight checks against the five laws of melodic
memory and the prosody diagnostic), and the Approach Design (a
specification of the pre-hook suspension for each chorus entrance).

## 23.2 The Hook Specification

Every song must have an explicit hook specification before the engine
proceeds to production. The specification has four required components:
location (which section, which beat, which phrase), melodic feature
(what the melody does at the hook --- the specific interval, contour, or
rhythmic figure that makes it distinctive), lyric content (the word or
phrase that the melody carries at the hook), and compound elements
(which additional channels are engaged: rhythmic, timbral, harmonic).

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  *Hook Specification Format: "The hook lands at [location]. The melody
  [does what]. The lyric says [what]. The compound elements are
  [rhythm / timbre / harmony / instrumentation]." Example: "The hook
  lands at the first word of the chorus, beat one. The melody leaps a
  major sixth from the last syllable of the pre-chorus and holds the high
  note for two beats before stepping down. The lyric says the title

## 23.4 The Approach Design

The approach is the pre-hook suspension: the musical material in the
final four to eight measures before the hook lands that activates the
caudate nucleus's anticipatory dopamine release. The approach has three
required elements.

Element 1: The Withheld Resolution

The harmonic or melodic resolution the hook will deliver must be
withheld for a measurable duration before the hook arrives. This
requires a pre-hook harmonic suspension --- typically a dominant seventh
chord, a suspended fourth voicing, or a ii-V turnaround --- held for at
least two measures before the tonic arrives at the hook. The longer the
withholding, the stronger the caudate release during anticipation. The
outer limit of productive withholding is approximately four measures in
congregational music; beyond that, the listener's attention may wander
rather than focus.

Element 2: The Elongated Approach Note

The note directly preceding the hook's peak note should be held longer
than expected --- typically one to two beats longer than the surrounding
phrase rhythm would predict. This temporal elongation increases the
tension response in Huron's ITPRA model and signals to the listener's
nervous system that something significant is arriving. The approach note
does not need to be dramatic; it needs to be held.

Element 3: The Dynamic or Textural Build

The approach should include a gradual increase in either dynamic level,
textural density, or both. A pre-chorus that strips texture before the
chorus adds it back produces a sharper contrast at the hook's arrival
than a pre-chorus that simply maintains the same level. A pre-chorus
that gradually adds a single new element --- a second guitar, a backing
vocal, a rising bass line --- while the primary vocal holds back
produces a build toward the hook that the body tracks as motion even
before the hook arrives.

## Principle 23: The Transcendent Level

Every song in the engine is designed across three emotional levels: the
pleasure of pattern, the reward of departure, and the transcendent
level. The first two levels are managed by the engine's existing
apparatus. The third is not achievable by any apparatus --- but it can
be served by asking the right questions at the right moments.

The transcendent level is the emotional register where music does not
merely please but changes. Where the listener after is not the same as
the listener before. Where the song carries something the listener did
not have before they heard it, and will carry with them after the song
ends.

This level is reached through four instruments: kama muta content (lyric
and narrative depicting communal love, sacrifice, or devotion at a
cost), awe and vastness (the song addressing something larger than any
individual life), intermediate originality calibrated to Simonton's
immortality curve, and the inevitable surprise (a hidden logic revealed
at the climactic moment).

> *The transcendent level is not the reward for doing the other levels
> correctly. It is the reason the other levels exist. The departure
> budget serves frisson. Frisson serves kama muta. Kama muta and awe
> together serve the experience that changes the listener. The
> engineer's tools are not the destination. The destination is the
> moment when the listener sits in silence after the music stops,
> because there is nothing else to say.*

Corollary: the transcendent level cannot be forced. But it can be
blocked. A song that is technically perfect but emotionally evasive ---
that constructs a beautiful hook over a lyric that names nothing true
and costs nothing to say --- will never reach Level 4. The engine's
structural apparatus serves the truth. It cannot replace it.

chorus's type-token ratio is below the verse's in 86% of songs; on the

the floor.

The last word of every chorus is the convergence word. It must: (1) end
on an open vowel or liquid consonant; (2) be one syllable if possible;
(3) land on the structural tone (scale degree 5) and be held 3--5
seconds; (4) be marked [HOLD] in all documentation.

The song establishes a point-of-view contract in the first verse and
must honor it throughout. An unannounced POV shift mid-chorus that
changes whose interior the listener is in is a structural failure.

The chorus melody is fixed from the first occurrence. The final chorus
is the inversion: same melody, singer now knows what the first singer
did not.

Same melody, same convergence word, different singer or knowledge state.

The bridge is the rupture. It must be the single most exposed moment in

# MODULE 21: BLUES SONG TEMPLATE (TYPE B)

## 21.1 Overview

The blues is the most widely influential song type in the history of
Western popular music. Jazz, rock, rhythm and blues, country, gospel,
and hip-hop all draw structural and harmonic vocabulary from it. The
engine has been building on the blues in every module without having a
blues module. This template provides that foundation.

The blues is not a mood. It is an architecture. A songwriter choosing
the blues is choosing a specific structural system with its own harmonic
laws, lyric form, rhythmic logic, frisson mechanism, and psychological
stance. The engine's job is to specify that system precisely enough that
a songwriter can work it consciously rather than accidentally.

## 21.3 Intake Protocol: B1--B5

B1 --- Identify the Subtype

Which subtype fits the context? Delta (exposed, personal, minimal),
Chicago (communal, full band, groove-forward), Jazz (harmonically
sophisticated), or Blues-Rock (intense, defiant, heavier)? If uncertain:
what is the instrumentation, and where does the suffering live in the
body --- the gut (Delta), the chest and room (Chicago), the head (Jazz),
or the legs and chest simultaneously (Blues-Rock)?

B2 --- Name the Suffering

What is this blues about? The blues lyric requires a specific subject:
not sadness in general, but this particular loss, injustice, longing, or
difficulty. The blues does not traffic in abstractions. "I got the
blues" is not a blues lyric. "It's three o'clock in the morning and I
can't close my eyes" is a blues lyric. The Q0 answer from the triage
protocol is the starting point. What specifically is the suffering? Name
it with the precision that would allow someone who has not experienced
it to recognize their own version of it.

B3 --- Find the Ironic Twist

Every strong blues verse contains a turn in the B line that is neither
simple complaint nor transcendence. It is defiant acknowledgment ---
often ironic, sometimes darkly comic, always refusing to be crushed. The
B line answers the two A lines with something unexpected: a consequence
that reveals the absurdity of the situation, a survival despite all
evidence, a moment of wit in the middle of genuine pain. If the B line
has no twist --- if it simply restates the suffering more intensely ---
the verse is incomplete.

B4 --- Establish the Physical Stance

The blues singer inhabits a specific physical relationship to the
material. Not the weeping of the lament. Not the ecstasy of the groove.
Something closer to a steady, grounded presence: eyes open, feet
planted, voice level, body still moving. The convergence tone should
feel like standing one's ground rather than breaking open. What is the
physical posture this song demands? The answer determines tempo, groove
tightness, and the dynamic ceiling.

B5 --- Determine the Verse Count

The blues has no chorus. Each verse is complete. The song does not build
toward a climax --- it deepens. Each subsequent verse adds specificity,
complication, or a new angle on the same suffering. A standard blues has
three to five verses. The final verse does not resolve anything; it
typically delivers the most concentrated or pointed statement of the
stance. The ending is not arrival. It is the most recent return of the
cycle.

## 21.4 Lyric Architecture

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  AAB form. Each verse complete. No chorus. No arc. The B line is the
  answer, the twist, the defiance.

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------

The A lines: Statement and Weight

The first A line makes a statement about the situation. The second A
line repeats it with a slight variation that adds weight. The repetition
is not laziness. In the blues, repetition enacts the persistence of the
situation: it was true the first time, it is still true the second time,
it is not going away. The repetition is the formal shape of the
suffering itself.

Both A lines must be specific. Not "I've got troubles" but "I woke up
this morning, found my baby gone." Not "life is hard" but "I got
thirty-seven cents and the landlord at my door." The specificity is what
creates recognition frisson.

The B line: The Defiant Answer

21.7a The Hold Against a Feminine Title (v47, fix 3.1). When the
title or a line ends on an unstressed syllable ('MORN-ing'), the
convergence tone --- and any hold --- lands on the last stressed
syllable and is held there; the unstressed syllable that follows repeats
the pitch, short (0.5 beat), on the last half-beat before the bar line,
never on a strong beat. The joins rule (v43) and this rule now agree: a
note of a beat or more goes only on a stressed syllable, and the
feminine tail is never a hold.

21.7a amended (v60, Window 78, fix 7): the feminine tail before a
pickup. 21.7a put the tail of a feminine ending on the eighth after
the held stress, and song 16's chorus hooks end on tails ('-ter',
'-er') with the next line's pickup on the eighth before the bar line:
the run's first fallback cut the hook's hold to an eighth to make
room. The fallback is now stated: when the next line's first note would
collide with the tail, the tail moves to the latest free eighth before
it that is not a strong beat (1 or 3) --- a breath (0.5 beat) and the
tail (0.5 beat) before the next onset --- and the stressed note HOLDS up
to it; only when no such eighth exists does the tail take the eighth
after the stress. A tail on 4-and before a pickup on 4-and moves to
3-and and the hold loses one eighth, not all of them; every move is
logged (tails).

21.7a amended again (v66, Window 84, song 32 fix 105): a designed
anchor's waiver. 21.7a keeps a feminine tail on its stress's pitch
even on a designed anchor: song 32's 'Ma-ry' sits on F♯5 for both
syllables as designed ('as he would say it'), though a falling third
is the natural spoken call (song 29's 'Ab-ba'). A designed anchor may
WAIVE 21.7a with a logged reason, and the evaluation reads the waiver;
the writer chooses.

21.4a The Twist, Measured (v47, fix 1.3). The B line of the AAB
verse is a turn: it reverses, literalizes or reframes the A line. Module
28.10 measures it and gates the keepers of a slot marked as a turn; turn
lines are exempt from Rule V1 --- 'they hold on and I let go' is the
form working, not a missing picture.

The B line is the structural pivot of the blues verse. Strong blues B
lines do one of three things: name the ironic consequence (the suffering
produces an absurd or unexpected outcome); announce continued presence
despite the suffering; or deliver a sudden shift in angle that
recontextualizes everything that came before. The B line creates the
feeling of resolution without actually resolving anything.

> *The B line is the blues' answer to its own question. It does not say:
> the suffering is gone. It says: I am still here, and here is what I
> notice about that.*

Three Lyric Rules

Rule B-1 --- Name the Specific: Every verse must name one concrete,
physical, specific detail of the suffering. Not the category of loss but
the instance of it.

Rule B-2 --- No False Transcendence: The blues does not end with the
suffering overcome or transformed into joy. If the verse ends with the
singer feeling better about their situation, it has left the blues.
Route to Lament (seeking God's response) or Narrative (telling how
things improved).

Rule B-3 --- The Twist Earns the Form: The B line must shift the angle
through surprise, irony, or specificity the A lines could not predict. A
B line that only intensifies the A lines has failed structurally.

## 21.7 Convergence Tone

The blues convergence tone communicates standing one's ground. The held
note at emotional peak should be the flat seventh (♭7) or the flat third
(♭3) --- the blue note zones where major and minor are simultaneously
present. The hold is not a sob and not a shout. It is a statement: this
is the pitch I am standing on, and I am not moving from it.

The B line's final syllable, held into the beginning of the turnaround,
is the characteristic blues frisson moment. The turnaround then pulls
the harmonic ground forward into the next verse while the voice is still
sustaining. The body registers this as the cycle continuing even while
this moment is still in progress.

## 21.9 Frisson Mechanism

The blues produces frisson through three mechanisms in order of
frequency: (1) Recognition frisson --- the B line names the twist or
irony the listener did not anticipate but immediately recognizes as

final syllable, especially when sustained into the turnaround; (3)
Instrumental response frisson --- the moments when the guitar, harp, or
horn answers the voice in the call-and-response gap with a phrase that
seems to know exactly what the voice just said.

## 21.11 The Blues and the Engine's Architecture

The blues is the ancestor of the engine's rock module (9-R). The
dominant seventh tonic, the plagal resolution, the blue note, the
shuffled groove, the instrumental call-and-response, the specific stance
toward suffering as something to be inhabited rather than escaped ---
all of these passed from the blues into rock, R&B, gospel, soul, and
country. The engine now has the source.

Blues hybridizes naturally with Lament when the suffering is addressed
to God rather than endured directly --- the spiritual and gospel
traditions are at this intersection. Blues hybridizes with Groove when
the lyric content is lighter and the physical pleasure of the shuffle is
the primary payload --- boogie, early R&B, and dancehall blues live
here. When either hybrid is the actual intent, name the primary type and
apply the secondary type's constraints as a budget modifier.

# MODULE 22: GOSPEL / TESTIMONY SONG TEMPLATE (TYPE T)

## 22.1 Overview

The testimony song is the engine's oldest song type and its last to be
fully specified. "Amazing Grace" is a testimony song. So is "Oh Happy
Day," "At the Cross," and "My Testimony" by Elevation Worship. The form
has been producing culturally transformative songs for over two
centuries because it does something structurally that no other song type
does: it makes a personal transformation into a communal offer.

The testimony song is not the Narrative type (which tells stories
without necessarily inviting the listener into them) or the Worship type
(which addresses God rather than the congregant). It is the form in
which personal experience becomes evangelistic witness: a first-person
account of transformation extended toward a second person who might

## 22.3 Intake Protocol: T1--T5

T1 --- Identify the Subtype

Personal (T/P): intimate, solo, specific story. Congregational (T/C):
full ensemble, vamp is the centerpiece, the personal becomes communal.
Hymnic (T/H): formal strophic structure, multiple verses of equal
weight. Invitation (T/I): the testimony is minimal, the offer is
everything. The subtype determines whether the vamp is the structural
climax (T/C), whether verse accumulation is the primary architecture
(T/H), whether emotional openness of invitation dominates (T/I), or
whether the specific personal story is the primary payload (T/P).

T2 --- Name the Before State

What was the condition before transformation? The answer must be
specific. Not "I was broken." The specific quality of the lostness: the
particular loneliness, the specific weight, the texture of the
emptiness. This is the most important intake question. The testimony
song's power to produce recognition in the listener is entirely
dependent on the specificity of the before state. The more particular
the darkness, the more universal the light.

T3 --- Name the Encounter

What was the felt quality of the transformation? Not a theological
explanation but the specific felt quality: "amazing grace," "love lifted
me," "grace rewrote my story." The encounter is the hinge of the song.
It must be specific enough to feel real and simple enough to be sung.
Overcomplicated theology at this moment kills the song.

T4 --- Locate the Invitation

Where does the second-person address appear? In the bridge? In a final
verse? Woven into the chorus? It must be structurally explicit. "This
grace is for you." "You can know this freedom." Without the
second-person address, the testimony song has not done what it is for.
The invitation is the structural completion of the form.

T5 --- Design the Vamp Architecture (for T/C)

For the congregational subtype, the vamp requires explicit design
decisions. What is the vamp material --- a short declaration from the
chorus, a single phrase from the bridge, or a new condensed refrain? How
many modulations are planned and at what interval? What is the soloist's
improvisational role over the vamp ground? Where does the congregation
fully join? The vamp is the structural climax of T/C and must be
designed, not discovered by accident.

## 22.4 Lyric Architecture

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  Verse: past tense evidence. Chorus: present tense claim. Bridge:
  universalizing turn or explicit invitation. Vamp: communal
  incorporation.

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------

The Verse: Evidence

The verse is past tense. It has two mandatory components: the before
state (named with specificity) and the encounter (named with
simplicity). Every element is chosen for its power to create recognition
in the listener and establish the ground for the chorus's declaration.
Any verse line that is a present-tense declaration belongs in the
chorus.

The Chorus: The Claim

The chorus is present tense: who the singer now is and what they now
know. The chorus must be singable by the whole room --- a functional
constraint, not a preference. The testimony song's climax is the room
claiming the identity together, not the soloist demonstrating it. Vocal
range ceiling: no higher than E5 for the congregational melody.

The Bridge: The Turn

The bridge universalizes the testimony (moving from personal experience
to shared truth) and/or issues the explicit invitation. The bridge is
not a third verse continuing the narrative; it shifts the register ---
higher energy, higher pitch, or a new harmonic perspective. Without the
bridge's universalizing or inviting move, the testimony remains personal
autobiography.

Three Lyric Rules

Rule T-1 --- Earn the Chorus Through the Verse: The chorus declaration
is only as strong as the before-state naming in the verse is honest and
specific. A vague verse produces a lightweight chorus.

Rule T-2 --- The Invitation Must Be Explicit: The second-person address
must appear in the song. If the listener cannot hear the song addressing
them specifically, the testimony has remained the singer's story.

Rule T-3 --- The Chorus Belongs to the Room: The chorus melody must be
carried by ordinary voices. Melisma and vocal improvisation belong in
the vamp and verse approaches; the chorus must be immediately singable.

## 22.7 Convergence Tone

The testimony song's convergence tone is the chorus's peak declaration

the physical equivalent of what the text declares: the transformation is
real, the identity is claimed, the home is found.

In the vamp, the convergence tone shifts to the elevated key --- the
same pitch in the new tonal center, now brighter, now higher, now
receiving the room's full participation. The moment when the
congregation's collective voice is at maximum synchrony with the
declared truth is the vamp's ritual completion: the community has been
lifted to a place the verse could not reach alone.

## 22.9 Frisson Mechanism

The testimony song produces frisson through four mechanisms in order of
architectural significance: (1) Recognition frisson --- the before-state
naming in the verse produces the moment when the listener recognizes
their own version of the described condition; the primary frisson
mechanism and the reason verse specificity is the single most important
craft decision. (2) Arrival frisson --- the chorus's tonic arrival
produces the bodily experience of homecoming; the chord and the word
arrive together. (3) Communal convergence frisson --- the moment in the
vamp when the congregation's full participation synchronizes with the
soloist; this is a social frisson, the feeling of being one voice among
many claiming the same truth. (4) Elevating modulation frisson --- the
key change within the vamp arrives before conscious recognition and
produces a surge the body registers as lift.

## 22.11 The Testimony Song and the Engine's Architecture

The engine began as a project in sacred music. The testimony song was
present at the beginning as the reason for the project and is the last
type to receive its full specification.

It hybridizes with Lament (Module 14) when the before state is named
with the extended weight of a lament but the song moves through the turn
toward transformation. It hybridizes with Worship (Module 19) when the
chorus turns upward to God and the testimony creates the ground for
worship --- a T/W hybrid, with testimony as the vehicle and worship as
the destination. It hybridizes with Narrative (Module 13) in the hymnic
subtype (T/H), where multiple verses develop the testimony arc with the
formal discipline of a story song.

When any hybrid is the actual intent, name the primary type and apply
the secondary type's constraints as a budget modifier. The invitation
determines the primary type. If the second-person address is
structurally present and functions as the song's completion, the primary
type is T.

> *The testimony song is the engine's completion because it is the only
> type that asks something of the listener. Every other type says: here
> is what is true, here is what was felt, here is what happened. The
> testimony song says: this happened to me, and I am singing it to you,
> because it can happen to you too. That is the song the engine was
> built to help write.*

## Principle 22: The Approach Is the Hook

In every song the engine produces, the hook is the destination. But the
dopamine circuit fires twice: once during the approach and once at
arrival. The caudate nucleus releases dopamine in anticipation of the
emotional peak, and the nucleus accumbens releases dopamine at the peak
itself. This means the eight measures before the chorus drops are not
transition material. They are the first half of the dopamine event.

A hook with no approach delivers half the neurochemical reward. A hook
preceded by a well-designed suspension --- a withheld resolution, an
elongated pre-tonic note, a quietly building dynamic, a suspended
harmony over a pedal point --- delivers the full circuit. The listener's
body begins releasing dopamine before the hook lands. When the hook
arrives, it lands into a reward system that is already primed.

> *The approach earns the arrival. The arrival cannot earn itself.
> Design the suspension as deliberately as the hook. The moment before
> the hook is the hook starting.*

Corollary: the hook must be preceded by something that is not the hook.
A chorus that begins with the hook on beat one of measure one, with no
pre-chorus, no elongated approach, no suspended harmony, delivers the
hook cold into an unprimed system. It may still work. It will work less
well. The most memorable musical moments in recorded history --- the
piano intro of Let It Be, the guitar build before the chorus of Born to
Run, the elongated approach to the chorus of Total Eclipse of the Heart
--- are not hooks. They are the approaches to hooks. And they are
remembered as vividly as the hooks themselves, because they are the
first half of the same dopamine event.

Application across song types: every song type in the engine has a hook.
The paradox song's hook lives in the pivot word where the tension
resolves into acceptance. The lament's hook lives in the turn toward
trust. The gospel testimony's hook lives in the chorus declaration. The
anthem's hook lives in the collective pronoun on the high note. In every
case: design the approach. Name it. Measure it. The approach is the hook
starting.
